_about: Plant care profiles for anywhere in the US. Windows are relative to the location's median last spring frost / first fall frost (computed from its ZIP), so they shift automatically from Minnesota to Florida. 'zones' = USDA hardiness zones where the plant (or task) applies. Triggers use the same engine as the lawn program (see tools/lawn_engine.py). Any profile can also be used for a custom plant: '🌿 plants: spring-shrub=Grandma's lilac'.

trigger.basis: Soil at 2½" averaging {val} on {date}, about when forsythia blooms. Classic rose-pruning time.

tasks.note: Cut out dead/crossing canes and shape to 12–18" (Knock Outs to about 1/3 height). In zones 9–10, a lighter January trim.
Once new growth is a few inches long. Repeat every 4–6 weeks until the last feeding.
Stop fertilizing about 6–8 weeks before your first frost so growth hardens off.

tasks.task: Mound mulch over the base for winter

trigger.basis: Hard freeze (low {val}) on {trig}. Mound mulch now.

tasks.note: After the first hard freeze, mound 8–10" of mulch or compost over the crown. Don't prune now.

trigger.basis: Last frost was {since}; buds are leafing out, so dead wood is easy to see.

tasks.note: Wait until buds leaf out. Do NOT cut back healthy stems or you remove this year's flowers. Reblooming types (Endless Summer) are forgiving.

tasks.task: Deadhead / light shaping right after flowering
tasks.note: The only safe window for shaping. Next year's buds form by late summer, so no pruning after this.

tasks.task: Mulch the base; leave stems standing
tasks.note: 2–3" of mulch over the root zone protects the flower buds on the stems.
Blooms on new wood. Panicle: cut by about 1/3 to a strong framework. Smooth (Annabelle): cut to 12–18".

plants.name: Spring-flowering shrubs (lilac, forsythia, azalea, rhododendron, viburnum, spirea)

tasks.note: They set next year's flowers by midsummer, so prune within ~3 weeks of blooms fading. Renew by removing the oldest 1/3 of stems.
Only for acid-lovers (azalea, rhododendron, camellia, blueberry), right after bloom. Skip for lilac/forsythia.

plants.name: Summer-flowering shrubs (butterfly bush, rose of Sharon, summer spirea, abelia)

tasks.note: Blooms on new wood. Butterfly bush can be cut to 12–18"; others, shape and thin.

plants.name: Boxwood & hedges (privet, yew, holly, burning bush)

tasks.task: Shear after the spring growth flush
tasks.note: Keep the bottom wider than the top so it stays full. Boxwood: thin a few interior branches for airflow.
Light touch-up only. Later pruning pushes tender growth that winter burns.
Trim only new growth; most conifers won't regrow from bare old wood. Pines: pinch new 'candles' by half.

tasks.task: Deep watering before the ground freezes
tasks.note: Evergreens lose water all winter. Soak the root zone if fall has been dry.

plants.name: Shade trees (maple, oak, elm, redbud, birch)

tasks.note: Remove dead, crossing and low branches while dormant. OAKS: never prune April–July (oak wilt). Big limbs go to an arborist. Maples and birches may 'bleed' sap; that's harmless.
Trees planted in the last 3 years: about 10 gal per inch of trunk diameter every 2 weeks if dry.

plants.name: Fruit trees (apple, pear, peach, plum, cherry)

tasks.note: Open the center, remove water sprouts and crossing limbs. Prune peaches last.
Calm day above 40°F, no freeze for 24 hrs. Smothers overwintering scale, mites and aphid eggs.
Thin to one fruit every 6–8" for bigger fruit and less limb breakage.

trigger.basis: Last frost was {since}. Leaves are emerging, so dead wood shows.

tasks.note: Thin crossing branches and suckers; cut back only to live wood. Don't top them ('crape murder').

plants.name: Perennials (hosta, daylily, coneflower, salvia, black-eyed Susan, peony)

tasks.note: Cut last year's stems to the ground and divide overgrown clumps as shoots emerge. Top-dress with compost.

tasks.task: Fall cutback (leave seedheads for birds if you like)
tasks.note: After a hard freeze blackens foliage. Hostas, daylilies and peonies to the ground; coneflower and black-eyed Susan can stand for birds.
Before new shoots get tall. Tie big clumps with twine first for easy cleanup. Divide every 3–4 years.
Pinch the top 1" of each stem at 6" tall. Stop by early July or you lose fall flowers.
Wait until leaves yellow (about 6 weeks after bloom); they recharge next year's bulb.
Once soil cools below ~60°F, before the ground freezes. Plant 3× as deep as the bulb is tall. Zones 9+: buy pre-chilled bulbs and plant in December.
Once soil is 60°F+. Caladiums want 65°F+.

tasks.task: Dig and store tubers for winter

trigger.basis: First frost (low {val}) {trig} blackened the foliage, so it's time to lift.

tasks.note: After frost blackens the foliage: dig, dry a few days, store in peat or sawdust at 40–50°F. Zones 8+ can leave them in the ground.

tasks.task: Plant cool-season crops (peas, lettuce, spinach, onions, potatoes)
tasks.note: Soil 45°F+ and workable (not soggy). Light frosts are fine for these.
After the last frost with nights staying above 50°F. Harden off transplants for a week first.

tasks.task: Sow fall crops (lettuce, kale, spinach, radish, carrots)
tasks.note: Count back from frost: most greens need 50–60 days. Shade and water seedlings in late-summer heat.
Pull spent plants (toss diseased tomato vines; don't compost them), add compost or shredded leaves, mulch.
Pointy end up, 2" deep, 6" apart; mulch after the ground starts to freeze. Harvest next summer when half the leaves brown.
Blueberries: remove oldest canes and low twiggy growth. Raspberries: remove dead canes, thin to 4–6 per foot.

tasks.task: Feed after bloom (acid feed for blueberries)
tasks.note: Blueberries need acid fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or 'acid-loving'); others, a balanced feed.

tasks.task: Cut spent floricanes / renovate strawberries after harvest
tasks.note: Raspberries/blackberries: cut canes that fruited to the ground. June-bearing strawberries: mow leaves, thin, side-dress.
Citrus fertilizer with micronutrients. Repeat in late spring and late summer.
Second of three yearly feedings.

tasks.task: Late-summer citrus feeding (last of the year)
tasks.note: Last feeding so new growth hardens before cool weather.

tasks.task: Frost protection: cover or move inside

trigger.basis: Frost (low {val}) forecast {trig}. Cover, water the soil, or move pots inside.

tasks.note: Frost cloth to the ground (not touching leaves), water soil the day before, or bring containers into a garage.
Palm-specific slow-release with magnesium and potassium. Repeat about every 3 months through summer.
Never cut green or yellowing fronds; palms pull nutrients from them. No 'hurricane cuts'.

tasks.task: Prune and shape after frost risk
tasks.note: Cut back cold-damaged wood once frost risk is past, then shape. Feed as new growth starts.
Cover with frost cloth and water the soil before a frost night.

plants.name: Tender / container plants (tropicals, houseplants summering outside)

tasks.note: After the last frost with nights above 50°F. Start in shade for a week so leaves don't scorch.

trigger.basis: First frost (low {val}) forecast {trig}. Bring them in before then.

tasks.note: Before nights drop below about 45–50°F for tropicals. Check for pests and hose off first.
Containers leach nutrients fast: liquid feed every 2 weeks through summer, or slow-release once.
After the last frost. Pansies/violas can go in a month earlier; they like cool weather.

tasks.task: Swap in cool-season color (pansies, mums, kale)
tasks.note: Pull tired summer annuals; pansies planted now often bloom again in spring.
